appraisal_events.evidence: Seeing his wife come to speak to him, the duke put on so furious an expression that she could only withdraw; she tells the narrator, 'Il est occupé... nous verrons tout à l'heure', preferring to let him manage alone.
appraisal_events.explanation: A small public snub: the duke's visible fury forces the duchesse to retreat in front of the narrator, marking his dismissiveness toward her.

appraisal_events.evidence: The duchesse now dismisses Bréauté as merely 'un snob' and 'un voisin de campagne', not worth Bloch's interest, and the narrator adds that he has been 'entirely forgotten' by her, his name among those that 'no longer exist and, moreover, do not deserve to survive.'
appraisal_events.explanation: A man once treated as a central figure of Parisian society is shown reduced, in the duchesse's faded memory, to a forgettable provincial snob.

appraisal_events.evidence: The duchesse claims she personally 'discovered', championed, and 'launched' Rachel at a time when 'ma nouvelle cousine' -- Mme Verdurin, still just Mme Verdurin to Oriane despite her new title -- would have let her starve rather than listen to her.
appraisal_events.explanation: The duchesse claims credit and reflected prestige from Rachel's success while mocking Mme Verdurin as a former nobody unworthy of the credit, though the narrator has just shown how unreliably the duchesse's memory of the past has been reshaped to flatter her.

appraisal_events.evidence: Berma's son-in-law and daughter arrive uninvited begging to see Rachel perform; Rachel toys with them, first refusing, then admitting them with performed condescending kindness in front of a watching prince, 'ruining at a stroke Berma's social position as she had ruined her health', while secretly delighted to deal the Berma this blow.
appraisal_events.explanation: The scene stages a complete reversal of fortune: Rachel now holds the once-illustrious Berma's own children at her mercy and calculatedly delivers what the narrator frames as a devastating, possibly mortal, blow to Berma's standing.

status_effects.explanation: She is visibly rebuffed by her husband and forced to withdraw, a small but public loss of leverage in the marriage.
Once a notable figure, he is now recalled dismissively as a provincial snob not worth explaining.
Her claim to have discovered and launched Rachel casts her as an early, discerning patron, though the narrator's ironic framing leaves this self-flattering claim uncertain.
She is mocked by the duchesse as a pretended avant-gardist who would have let Rachel starve, and pointedly reduced to her old name.
The incident is framed as potentially a mortal blow, devastating her in her final, fragile days.
Rachel's public, witnessed reception of Berma's supplicant children ruins Berma's social position at a stroke.
Rachel visibly enacts and registers the reversal of fortune, condescendingly receiving the once-illustrious Berma's children before onlookers.
The narrator exposes Rachel's gracious performance as calculated and secretly gleeful cruelty toward a rival she has now surpassed.

ambiguities: The duchesse's claim to have 'launched' Rachel is delivered right after the narrator shows her memory of the past as unreliably reshaped to flatter her, so the sincerity and accuracy of the claim is left uncertain rather than endorsed at face value.
